newsitem.title: TRISTAN DA CUNHA: FEATURE-World's loneliest island, a paradise or a prison?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-World's loneliest island, a paradise or a prison?.
newsitem.dateline: EDINBURGH OF THE SEVEN SEAS, Tristan da Cunha 1997-01-23

text.p: To an outsider, the tiny South Atlantic island of Tristan da Cunha might seem like a paradise, but to its 320 inhabitants, it is in danger of becoming a prison.

The most remote inhabited island on the planet appears as a volcanic blister on the empty horizon midway between Africa and South America. Its sister island, Napoleon's exile home St Helena, is about 2,000 sea miles away.

"People don't leave the island because there is nowhere for them to go at the moment. They have no right of work elsewhere, neither in the United Kingdom nor in South Africa," island administrator Brendan Dalley said in an interview.
British anxiety about a mass migration from Hong Kong when it is handed back to China later this year has spawned a policy that puts Tristanians under virtual house arrest.

Hong Kong's millions, St. Helena's thousands and Tristan's hundreds share the "dependency" status that allows citizens to carry British passports, but denies them the right to live or work in the United Kingdom.
Along with the island's healthy economy, the citizenship status of Tristan's seven families was a major topic of debate during British Governor David Smallman's annual visit.

This month, he spent three days on the eight mile-wide island halfway between Cape Town and Buenos Aires, climbing the cliffs that guard the settlement plain and exploring the lifestyle of the people who see perhaps a dozen ships a year.

"Tristan has been epitomised as a paradise on earth, where everyone helps everyone else, and that is really the case still. But the young people are getting itchy feet and I think they deserve to be able to take advantage of some of the benefits of the last years of the 20th century," he said in an interview.
"The status they now hold is that of a British dependent citizen, which was framed by parliament essentially to contain the potential problem were Hong Kong to revert to China."
"NO CONSTITUENCY" IN BRITAIN

Smallman promised in an address to young islanders to fight to expand their right of access to the United Kingdom, saying he had already discussed the issue with British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind.
But he warned that no change was likely under the present government and said the next might be reluctant to rewrite the rules too soon after the Hong Kong issue is settled.
"There is no political constituency for us, nor any major incentive for a British government to make amends, even when Hong Kong has been handed over to China," he told them.
Smallman's first target is to win the right for Tristanians to serve alongside their cousins from St. Helena in the British armed forces and he is optimistic about early success.

The islanders, for whom the everyday world is a two square mile lava plain on the edge of a volcanic peak, are proudly self-sufficient, asking for nothing more than contract work away from their small settlement.

"We would like to have the opportunity to go, but I don't think that everybody would leave Tristan. If five islanders wished to go, I think that would be a lot," elected Chief Islander Jimmy Glass said.
FEWER RIGHTS THAN EU-MEMBERS

Glass is frank about the hurt he feels that a Frenchman or a Greek, as citizens of the European Union, enjoys more rights in Britain than a Tristanian who walks to work every day past a Union Jack fluttering in the centre of their town, Edinburgh of the Seven Seas.

"We've been flying the British flag since 1816...We consider ourselves British," he said in his sitting room, where a signed photograph of former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher and the dried jaws of a shark stand out amongst the decorations.
Glass is a descendant of the island's original settler, William Glass of Kelso in Scotland. The community counts seven surnames reflecting its Irish, English, Italian and Dutch founders.

They were evacuated to Britain in 1961 when the side of their apparently dormant volcano split and lava poured to the edges of the town, but they elected to return two years later and all but a handful have stayed.
Amanda Swain, young secretary to the manager of the island's single shop, said she would like to see the outside world, but not to leave for good.
"If I was to leave Tristan, I really would miss my home town. I'd always come back," she said.
PROUD AND SELF-SUFFICIENT

Apart from a respite from the relentless interdependence the island life imposes, Tristanians see a job contract away more as a means to learn new skills than as an opportunity to bring additional money to their economy.
They balance their budget, contribute to a growing reserve, produce enough meat, fish and vegetables to live on and cherish their immunity from ills such as crime, child abuse and drugs.
"We're literally self-sufficient... We are happy and proud to be self-sufficient," said Glass.

Already, Tristanians have taken over the jobs of expatriate department heads. A fisheries officer who reports to Glass, a doctor and the British-appointed administrator are the only posts still routinely filled by outsiders.
Tristan's 500,000 pound annual income comes mainly from the export of lobster to Japan and the United States, with about 40,000 pounds more from the sale of their prized stamps.

Last year, the island put its 340-tonne lobster concession out to tender for the first time in 48 years and awarded the 10-year contract to Premier Fishing, a subsidiary of South Africa's Premier Foods group, from January 1.

Premier Fishing director Brian Flanagan, who travelled to Tristan da Cuhna on the Royal Mail Ship St. Helena's annual visit, said he planned also to explore options to bring more work to the island's small processing and freezing factory.
"We want to give something back to Tristan, rather than just take their lobster and sell it," he said.
